title: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth
hook: before he dies the Guru tells the Sikhs that the scripture is now their Guru
carry: the book is the guru now

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama, the letter of victory, sent to an emperor. Your line was victory is the truth. Did you find your one honest sentence? Day ninety-three.

Every family knows the question nobody wants to ask out loud. When the one who holds us together is gone, who decides? Who do we go to? For more than two hundred years, the Sikhs always had an answer: the next Guru. Nanak chose Angad. Angad chose Amar Das. Nine times the light was handed on, person to person. Now it's 1708. Guru Gobind Singh is far from Punjab, in the south of India, at a town called Nanded on the Godavari river. He is wounded, and he knows he is dying. His four sons are gone. Everyone around him is waiting for the name. And the answer he gives is not a person.
screen: `WHO DO WE GO TO NOW?` → `NINE TIMES, PERSON TO PERSON.` → `NANDED, 1708.`

segments.voice: Guru Granth Sahib. Guru, the one who leads from darkness to light. Granth, a book, a volume. Sahib, a word of respect, like lord or master. Here's what happened, as Sikhs tell it. At Nanded, an assassin stabbed the Guru. The wound was stitched, and then it tore open again. Before he died, in October 1708, he gathered the Sikhs, and he bowed before the scripture: the Adi Granth that Guru Arjan had compiled, the one you met on day sixty-two, with the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur now added. And he told them that after him there would be no more human Gurus. The Word in this book was their Guru. The authority of the community, the Khalsa gathered together, would stand alongside it. Sikhs call these two the Guru Granth and the Guru Panth. Think how bold that is. Nobody could inherit it, buy it, or fight over it. The Guru is now the same for everyone, and it speaks in the hymns of the Gurus and of saints from other backgrounds too. That's why a gurdwara looks the way it does. The Granth sits on a raised throne, under a canopy. Someone waves a whisk over it, the way you would for a king. At night it's carried to its own room to rest, and brought out again at dawn. It isn't treated like a book on a shelf. It's treated the way you'd treat a living teacher, because that's what Sikhs say it is. And after every Ardas, many congregations sing a couplet that says it plainly: all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as the Guru.
screen: `A WOUND THAT TEARS OPEN.` · `NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `THE GRANTH AND THE PANTH.` · `TREATED AS A LIVING TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE BOOK IS THE GURU NOW.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka, a small prayer book, or the Guru Granth Sahib itself, open it now. If you don't, open a page of it online, or just picture one: the wide page, the Gurmukhi script. Don't try to read it all. Let your eyes rest on one line. If you can understand it, stay with its meaning. If you can't, stay with its shape. Sikhs say this is how the Guru still speaks: one line, to one person, today. The bell holds the time.
Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, which Guru Gobind Singh named as the Guru for all time. The tenth Guru was the last human one.
Your line: the book is the guru now. Today, open the Granth, or a page of it, and read one line slowly, as if it were said to you. Day ninety-three.

howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib is installed each morning on a raised throne under a canopy and put to rest at night, and a daily hukamnama, a line chosen by opening it at random, is read out as the Guru's word for the day.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the Guru, the book, with a word of respect.

trapdoor: what you thought: the holy book Sikhs read from.
what it means: the living Guru of the Sikhs, since Guru Gobind Singh named it so at Nanded in 1708.
what a scholar hears: the Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, with Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns added, and authority shared with the Guru Panth, the Khalsa gathered.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on the passing of Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded, October 1708, and the naming of the Granth as Guru
the couplet sung after Ardas commanding Sikhs to accept the Granth as Guru

notes: Date of passing: 7 October 1708 in most accounts (some give 6/7 October). The script says 'October 1708'. Confirm.
The assassin (often named Jamshed Khan or Gul Khan) is not named; wound reopened: tradition. Confirm.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns added by Guru Gobind Singh (Damdama recension, c. 1706): stated in one clause. Confirm.
The couplet after Ardas ('Sabh Sikhan ko hukam hai, Guru manio Granth'): its later origin is debated by historians; the script says only that many congregations sing it. Confirm.
Guru Granth and Guru Panth described together; confirm balance.
Etymology of 'guru' as the one who leads from darkness to light is a traditional explanation; confirm it is acceptable to state.
